sections.title: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things

blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher. Standards and tools change (OWASP Top 10 editions, TLS versions, certificate exams), so check the official source named in the text before relying on a detail. Practise only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

Beginners (and some code reviewers) mix these up, and the mistake becomes a vulnerability.

| | Purpose | Reversible? | Needs a key? | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Encoding** | change the format so data fits a medium | yes, by anyone | no | Base64, URL encoding, hex |
| **Hashing** | a fixed-size fingerprint | **no** | no (HMAC does) | SHA-256, SHA-3, bcrypt for passwords |
| **Encryption** | hide data from anyone without the key | yes, with the key | yes | AES, ChaCha20, RSA |

`YWRtaW46cGFzc3dvcmQ=` is **Base64** of `admin:password`. It hides nothing. HTTP Basic authentication is exactly this, which is why it must only travel over HTTPS. If you find passwords "protected" by Base64 in a code review, that is a finding.

A hash function maps any input to a fixed-size output. The properties that matter:

- **Deterministic:** the same input always gives the same output.
- **Pre-image resistance:** given a hash, you cannot find an input that produces it.
- **Second pre-image resistance:** given one input, you cannot find a different input with the same hash.
- **Collision resistance:** you cannot find any two inputs with the same hash.
- **Avalanche effect:** changing one bit of input changes about half the output bits.

| Algorithm | Output | Status |
|---|---|---|
| MD5 | 128 bits (32 hex characters) | **broken** for collisions. Do not use for security |
| SHA-1 | 160 bits (40 hex) | **broken** for collisions (a practical collision was shown in 2017). Being retired |
| SHA-256 | 256 bits (64 hex) | secure, the general-purpose default |
| SHA-512 | 512 bits (128 hex) | secure |
| SHA-3 | 224 to 512 bits | secure, a different design from SHA-2 |

The **birthday bound** says collisions in an n-bit hash appear after about 2^(n/2) attempts, so a 128-bit hash gives only about 64 bits of collision security.

**Uses of hashing:** file integrity (published checksums), digital signatures (sign the hash, not the whole file), Git commit IDs, deduplication and, with extra care, password storage.

### HMAC: a hash with a key

A plain hash proves nothing about who made it, because anyone can compute it. **HMAC** mixes a secret key into the hash: `HMAC(key, message)`. Only holders of the key can produce or verify the tag, which gives **integrity and authenticity**. Webhooks, API request signing and JWTs with `HS256` all use HMAC-SHA-256. Always compare tags with a **constant-time** function to avoid timing leaks.

- **Lengths:** MD5 128 bits = 32 hex, SHA-1 160 = 40 hex, SHA-256 256 = 64 hex, SHA-512 512 = 128 hex.
- **Broken for collisions:** MD5 and SHA-1. Use SHA-256 or better.
- **Collision effort:** about 2^(n/2) for an n-bit hash.
- **Hash is not encryption:** you cannot "decrypt" a hash, you can only guess and compare.
- **Need to prove who sent it?** Use HMAC (shared key) or a digital signature (private key).
blocks.title: Hash cheat codes

blocks.text:
One **shared secret key** both encrypts and decrypts. It is fast, so it carries the bulk of the data. The hard part is sharing the key safely.

- **AES** is the standard block cipher. Block size is always **128 bits**. Key sizes are **128, 192 or 256 bits**. DES (56-bit key) is broken and 3DES is deprecated.
- **ChaCha20-Poly1305** is a modern stream cipher with authentication, common on phones and in TLS 1.3.
- A **block cipher mode** says how to encrypt more than one block:

| Mode | Behaviour | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **ECB** | each block encrypted independently | **never use**: identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks and patterns leak (the famous encrypted penguin picture) |
| **CBC** | each block is XORed with the previous ciphertext, needs a random IV | acceptable but gives **no integrity** and has padding-oracle attacks if misused |
| **CTR** | turns the cipher into a stream cipher | fast, also no integrity |
| **GCM** | CTR plus an authentication tag (**AEAD**) | **the default choice**: encrypts and detects tampering |

- An **IV or nonce** is a non-secret value that makes each encryption different. For **GCM the nonce must never repeat under the same key**, because a repeat breaks both secrecy and authenticity.
- **Encryption without authentication** allows an attacker to flip bits in the ciphertext and change the plaintext in a predictable way. Use an AEAD mode.
- **Key length vs password:** an AES key is random bytes, a password is not. To derive a key from a password use a slow function (PBKDF2, scrypt or Argon2).

blocks.title: AES-256-GCM with the Java standard library

blocks.text: Use a reviewed library (the JDK, Bouncy Castle, Google Tink) and its high-level API. Never write your own cipher, never reuse a nonce, never hard-code a key in source code, and never use `java.util.Random` for anything secret. Use `SecureRandom`.
blocks.title: Do not invent crypto

blocks.text:
Each party has a **key pair**: a public key that can be shared and a private key that never leaves its owner. What one key does, only the other can undo.

| Goal | Use | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | encrypt with the **recipient's public key**, they decrypt with their private key | |
| **Authenticity and non-repudiation** | **sign with your private key**, anyone verifies with your public key | digital signature |
| **Agree on a shared key** | key exchange (Diffie-Hellman, ECDH) | both sides compute the same secret without sending it |

- **RSA** relies on the difficulty of factoring a large number n = p × q. Use at least **2048-bit** keys. **ECC** (elliptic curve cryptography) gives similar strength with far shorter keys: 256-bit ECC is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA. **Ed25519** and **ECDSA** are common signature schemes.
- Asymmetric operations are slow, so real systems use them only to **exchange a key or sign a hash**, and then switch to symmetric encryption. This is called **hybrid encryption** and it is what TLS does.
- **Digital signature flow:** hash the message, encrypt/sign the hash with the private key, send message and signature. The receiver hashes the message and checks the signature with the public key. A changed message gives a different hash and the check fails.

### Toy RSA: do this once to understand it

Take p = 61, q = 53 (real keys use primes of 1000+ bits).

1. n = p × q = **3233**
2. φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1) = 60 × 52 = **3120**
3. Choose e = **17** (coprime to 3120). Public key = (3233, 17).
4. d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) = **2753**. Private key = (3233, 2753).
5. Encrypt m = 65: c = 65¹⁷ mod 3233 = **2790**. Decrypt: 2790²⁷⁵³ mod 3233 = 65.

Textbook RSA like this is insecure without padding (OAEP for encryption, PSS for signatures). Real libraries add it for you.

### Diffie-Hellman in one example

Public values p = 23 and g = 5. Alice picks secret a = 6 and sends A = 5⁶ mod 23 = 8. Bob picks b = 15 and sends B = 5¹⁵ mod 23 = 19. Alice computes 19⁶ mod 23 = 2. Bob computes 8¹⁵ mod 23 = 2. They share the secret **2** and an eavesdropper who saw only 23, 5, 8 and 19 cannot easily get it. Unauthenticated DH is open to a man-in-the-middle, which is why certificates are needed.

- **Encrypt to someone:** their **public** key. **Sign as yourself:** your **private** key.
- **Verify a signature:** the signer's **public** key.
- **Private key leaked = start over:** revoke, reissue, rotate.
- **Sizes:** RSA ≥ 2048 bits, ECC 256 bits (≈ RSA 3072), AES 128 or 256 bits.
- **Hybrid:** asymmetric for the key exchange or signature, symmetric (AES-GCM) for the data.
blocks.title: Public-key cheat codes

blocks.text:
**TLS** (Transport Layer Security) protects HTTP and many other protocols. It gives **confidentiality** (encryption), **integrity** (authentication tags) and **server authentication** (a certificate).

### How a TLS 1.3 connection starts

1. **ClientHello:** the client sends supported versions and cipher suites and its key share.
2. **ServerHello and certificate:** the server picks the options, returns its key share and its **certificate**, and proves it owns the private key.
3. Both sides derive the same session keys using (EC)DHE, then switch to symmetric encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305).

- **Forward secrecy:** because every session uses fresh ephemeral DH keys, stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt recorded old traffic. TLS 1.3 makes this mandatory.
- **Versions:** SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are obsolete and should be disabled. Use **TLS 1.2 and 1.3**. TLS 1.3 removes old weak options and completes the handshake in one round trip.
- **mTLS (mutual TLS):** the server also demands a client certificate. Common between internal services.

### Certificates and certificate authorities

An **X.509 certificate** binds a public key to an identity (a domain name) and is signed by a **certificate authority (CA)**. Browsers and operating systems ship a list of trusted **root CAs**. A server usually presents a **chain**: its own certificate, signed by an intermediate CA, signed by a root.

A client accepts a certificate only if all of these hold:

- the chain leads to a **trusted root** and every signature is valid,
- the certificate is **within its validity dates** and not **revoked** (CRL or OCSP),
- the **domain name matches** the Subject Alternative Name,
- the certificate may be used for this purpose.

blocks.code: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
blocks.title: Looking at a certificate (any site you are allowed to connect to)

blocks.text:
- **Let's Encrypt** issues free, automated certificates that last 90 days and renew automatically.
- **HSTS** (`Strict-Transport-Security` header) tells the browser to use HTTPS only for a domain, so an attacker cannot downgrade the connection.
- **Self-signed certificates** are fine for local development but give no third-party proof of identity. Never tell users to click through a certificate warning.
- **Certificate pinning** ties a client to a specific key or certificate. It is powerful but can break the app when keys rotate.

A password must never be stored in clear text or encrypted (encryption can be reversed if the key leaks). It must be stored as a **slow, salted hash**.

| Idea | Why |
|---|---|
| **Salt**: a random value (16 bytes or more) generated per user and stored with the hash | the same password gives different hashes, so precomputed **rainbow tables** are useless and one cracked hash does not reveal others |
| **Pepper**: a secret value kept outside the database (an HSM or secret store) | a stolen database alone is not enough to crack hashes |
| **Slow, memory-hard hashing** | a plain SHA-256 can be computed billions of times a second on a GPU. A deliberately slow function cuts that to thousands |

Use one of: **Argon2id** (first choice in OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet), **scrypt**, **bcrypt** (cost factor 10 or more) or **PBKDF2** (a very high iteration count). Check the cheat sheet for current parameters because hardware keeps improving. Spring Security's `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` stores the algorithm in the hash (`{bcrypt}$2a$10$...`), so you can upgrade algorithms later.

blocks.code:
PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);   // cost factor 12 = 2^12 rounds
String hash = encoder.encode(rawPassword);                 // the salt is generated and stored inside the hash
boolean ok = encoder.matches(rawPassword, hash);           // constant-time comparison
blocks.title: Spring Security password hashing

blocks.text:
### How strong is a password?

Entropy in bits = length × log₂(size of the alphabet), for a randomly chosen password.

| Password | Alphabet | Entropy |
|---|---|---|
| 8 random lowercase letters | 26 | 8 × 4.70 = **37.6 bits** |
| 8 random from letters and digits (62) | 62 | 8 × 5.95 = **47.6 bits** |
| 12 random from 94 printable characters | 94 | 12 × 6.55 = **78.7 bits** |
| 6 random Diceware words | 7776 | 6 × 12.9 = **77.5 bits** |

**Length beats complexity.** "Password1!" looks complex but is on every cracking list. A long random passphrase or a password manager beats a short symbol-filled word. Check passwords against lists of breached passwords, and do not force periodic changes without a reason (NIST SP 800-63B recommends against it).

- **Never** plain text, Base64, reversible encryption, or a fast hash such as MD5 or one round of SHA-256.
- **Always** a unique random **salt** per password and a **slow** algorithm: Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2.
- **Pepper** lives outside the database.
- **Entropy** = length × log₂(alphabet). Each extra random character is worth 5 to 6.5 bits.
- **Rainbow tables** are defeated by salts. **GPU cracking** is slowed by work factors.
- Reset passwords by a one-time, expiring link. Never e-mail the old password (you should not be able to).
blocks.title: Password storage cheat codes

blocks.text: DNS resolves the name. The client opens a TCP connection and sends a ClientHello. The server returns a certificate chain and a key share. The client validates the chain (trusted root, dates, name, revocation), both sides derive session keys with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, and everything afterwards is encrypted and authenticated with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. HSTS stops downgrade to HTTP.
blocks.title: "What happens when you type https://bank.com?"
Key points
blocks.text:
- Encoding is not encryption and hashing is not reversible
- Use SHA-256 or better, never MD5 or SHA-1 for security
- Use authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM and never reuse a nonce
- Encrypt to the public key, sign with the private key
- TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral key exchange for forward secrecy
- Store passwords with a salt and a slow algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt

55 original questions on 10 areas. *Recall* questions test a definition or a rule. *Scenario* questions give you a situation, a log or a snippet and ask what is wrong or what to do. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

items.q: *(Recall)* The string dXNlcjpwYXNz is found in a code review as "protected" credentials. It is most likely
o: Base64 encoding, which anyone can reverse
items.w: Base64 uses only letters, digits, + and / and is decoded without a key. This one decodes to user:pass. Encoding is not protection.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which statement is true?
o: hashing can be reversed with the right key
encoding and encryption are the same
encryption is reversible with the key, hashing is one-way
items.w: Encryption is designed to be undone by the key holder. A hash has no key to undo it. Encoding has no secret at all.

items.q: *(Recall)* HTTP Basic authentication sends credentials as
items.w: It is only encoding, so Basic authentication must always run over HTTPS.

items.q: *(Recall)* A SHA-256 digest written in hexadecimal has how many characters?
items.w: 256 bits / 4 bits per hex character = 64 characters.

items.q: *(Recall)* An MD5 digest written in hexadecimal has how many characters?
items.w: MD5 is 128 bits, which is 32 hex characters. SHA-1 gives 40 and SHA-256 gives 64.

items.q: *(Recall)* How many bits are in a SHA-512 digest?
items.w: The name is the size.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which hash function is currently considered unsuitable for security because practical collisions exist?
items.w: MD5 collisions have been practical for years and SHA-1 collisions were shown in 2017. Use SHA-256 or SHA-3.

items.q: *(Recall)* Changing one character of a file produces a completely different hash. This is called
items.w: Small input changes flip about half the output bits, so similar inputs cannot be recognised from their hashes.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Which is the beginning of SHA-256("abc")?
items.w: ba7816bf8f01cfea... is the well-known SHA-256 of abc. e3b0c442 is the hash of the empty string and 5e884898 is the hash of "password".

items.q: *(Recall)* The birthday bound says that finding a collision in an n-bit hash takes about
items.w: A 128-bit hash offers only about 64 bits of collision resistance, which is one reason 128-bit hashes are considered weak for signatures.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A software vendor publishes an installer and its SHA-256 hash on the same web page. Why is that weaker than it seems?
o: an attacker who can change the download can change the hash on the same page too
items.w: Integrity checks need a trusted channel for the hash or a digital signature. Otherwise the hash only catches accidental corruption.

items.q: *(Recall)* HMAC differs from a plain hash because it
o: mixes in a secret key, so only key holders can produce or verify the tag
items.w: A plain hash can be computed by anyone. An HMAC proves integrity and authenticity to someone who shares the key.

items.q: *(Scenario)* An API signs requests with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The server compares the received signature with the expected one using ==. What is the weakness?
o: HMAC cannot be used for APIs
a normal comparison can leak timing information, so a constant-time comparison should be used
items.w: Early-exit comparisons take slightly longer the more leading bytes match, letting an attacker recover a valid tag byte by byte. Use a constant-time compare such as MessageDigest.isEqual.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Two parties share the key "k". The HMAC-SHA256 of the message "pay 100" is computed by both. If an attacker changes the message to "pay 900" without the key, the receiver will
o: see that the tag does not match
items.w: The tag depends on the message and the key, so a modified message produces a different tag that the attacker cannot recompute.

items.q: *(Recall)* The block size of AES is
o: the same as the key size
items.w: AES always works on 128-bit blocks. The key can be 128, 192 or 256 bits.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which AES key length is NOT valid?
items.w: AES defines 128, 192 and 256-bit keys. 512 bits is a hash size and not an AES key size.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which of these ciphers should no longer be used?
items.w: DES has a 56-bit key and can be brute-forced. 3DES is deprecated as well.

items.q: *(Recall)* The major weakness of ECB mode is that
o: identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks, leaking patterns
items.w: Structure in the data, such as an image, remains visible in the ciphertext.

items.q: *(Recall)* AES-GCM is called an AEAD mode because it
o: provides confidentiality and integrity together, via an authentication tag
items.w: AEAD means authenticated encryption with associated data. Tampering is detected when decrypting.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A developer encrypts every message with AES-GCM using the same key and a fixed all-zero nonce. What is the problem?
o: reusing a nonce under one key breaks the confidentiality and authenticity guarantees of GCM
items.w: GCM requires a unique nonce for every encryption with the same key. Generate a fresh random 96-bit nonce or use a counter.

items.q: *(Scenario)* An encrypted cookie uses AES-CBC with no MAC. An attacker flips bits in the ciphertext and the server accepts it, with the decrypted value altered. Which property is missing?
items.w: CBC alone does not detect modification. Use AES-GCM or encrypt-then-MAC.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which Java class should be used to generate keys, nonces and tokens?
items.w: Random and Math.random are predictable. SecureRandom draws from the operating system's entropy source.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A one-time pad XOR operation: the byte 0x5A is XORed with the key byte 0x3C. The result is
items.w: 0101 1010 XOR 0011 1100 = 0110 0110, which is 0x66. XOR is its own inverse, so XORing again with 0x3C returns 0x5A.

items.q: *(Recall)* A Caesar cipher with shift 3 turns KHOOR back into
items.w: Each letter moves three places back: K→H, H→E, O→L, O→L, R→O. A Caesar cipher has only 25 useful keys and is trivial to brute-force.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why can a Caesar cipher not be considered secure?
o: the key space is tiny, so every shift can be tried in a moment
items.w: There are only 25 non-trivial shifts. Even a substitution cipher falls to letter-frequency analysis.

items.q: *(Recall)* To send a confidential message to Bob using public-key encryption, Alice encrypts with
items.w: Only Bob's private key can decrypt what Bob's public key encrypted.

items.q: *(Recall)* To create a digital signature, the signer uses
items.w: Anyone can then verify it with the signer's public key, and only the signer could have created it.

items.q: *(Recall)* A digital signature does NOT by itself provide
items.w: A signature proves who signed and that the data is unchanged. The message remains readable unless it is also encrypted.

items.q: *(Recall)* 256-bit elliptic-curve keys give roughly the security of an RSA key of
items.w: ECC achieves the same strength with much smaller keys, which makes it popular on phones and in TLS.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Textbook RSA with p = 61, q = 53 and public exponent e = 17. The private exponent d is
items.w: n = 3233 and φ(n) = 60 × 52 = 3120. d is the inverse of 17 modulo 3120, which is 2753 because 17 × 2753 = 46801 = 15 × 3120 + 1.

items.q: *(Scenario)* With the RSA key n = 3233, e = 17, the ciphertext of the message m = 65 is
items.w: c = m^e mod n = 65^17 mod 3233 = 2790. Decrypting with d = 2753 returns 65.

items.q: *(Scenario)* In a Diffie-Hellman exchange with p = 23, g = 5, Alice's secret a = 6 and Bob's secret b = 15, the shared secret is
items.w: Alice sends 5^6 mod 23 = 8 and Bob sends 5^15 mod 23 = 19. Alice computes 19^6 mod 23 = 2 and Bob computes 8^15 mod 23 = 2.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Plain Diffie-Hellman between two strangers is still vulnerable to
o: a man-in-the-middle, because neither side authenticates the other
brute force of small keys only
items.w: An active attacker can run one exchange with each party. Certificates or signatures are needed to authenticate the public values.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why do real systems encrypt bulk data with a symmetric cipher and not with RSA?
o: symmetric encryption is far faster, so public-key crypto is used only to exchange keys or sign hashes
items.w: This hybrid approach is what TLS does.

items.q: *(Recall)* Forward secrecy means
o: stealing the server's long-term private key later does not reveal past recorded sessions
items.w: Each session uses fresh ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys that are discarded afterwards. TLS 1.3 requires this.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which protocol versions should be disabled on a modern server?
items.w: Older versions have known weaknesses (POODLE, BEAST) and are deprecated. Use TLS 1.2 or 1.3.

items.q: *(Recall)* A TLS certificate binds
o: a public key to an identity such as a domain name, signed by a certificate authority
an IP address to a MAC address
items.w: The CA's signature is what lets a browser believe the key belongs to that domain.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A browser shows a certificate warning for shop.example.com. The certificate is valid and trusted, but it was issued for www.example.org. The problem is
o: a name mismatch: the certificate does not cover the site being visited
items.w: The name in the certificate (SAN) must match the host. A mismatch can mean a misconfiguration or a man-in-the-middle.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Users routinely click through a certificate warning on an internal tool. What is the risk?
o: they will also click through when an attacker presents a forged certificate, so MITM goes unnoticed
items.w: Training users to ignore warnings defeats server authentication. Fix the certificate instead (an internal CA trusted on the devices).

items.q: *(Recall)* HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) tells the browser to
o: always use HTTPS for the domain and refuse plain HTTP
items.w: It prevents downgrade and cookie-stripping attacks on later visits.

items.q: *(Recall)* Mutual TLS (mTLS) means
o: the client also presents a certificate and the server verifies it
items.w: It is widely used for service-to-service authentication.

items.q: *(Recall)* If a certificate authority's intermediate key is compromised, certificates it signed can be marked invalid through
items.w: Clients check revocation lists or OCSP responses where supported. Short-lived certificates reduce the need.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which is the right way to store a user's password?
o: encrypted with AES, key in the code
a salted hash made with a slow algorithm such as Argon2id, bcrypt or PBKDF2
items.w: Encryption is reversible if the key leaks, and a fast unsalted hash is cracked at billions of guesses per second.

items.q: *(Recall)* A salt is
o: a secret kept outside the database
a random per-user value stored with the hash that makes equal passwords hash differently
items.w: The secret kept outside the database is a pepper. A salt is not secret.

items.q: *(Recall)* Why are rainbow tables ineffective against salted hashes?
o: the table would have to be rebuilt for every salt
items.w: A precomputed table only works for one hash function without salt. A unique salt per user forces separate work for each hash.

items.q: *(Recall)* The cost factor of bcrypt is increased from 10 to 12. The work per hash becomes
items.w: The work is 2^cost, so cost 12 is 2^12 / 2^10 = 4 times more.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A breach exposes a table of unsalted SHA-1 password hashes. Which attack is now fastest?
o: looking the hashes up in precomputed tables of common passwords
items.w: Unsalted fast hashes of common passwords are in public lookup tables. The company should force resets and move to a salted slow hash.

items.q: *(Scenario)* The entropy of a random 8-character password using lowercase letters only, to the nearest bit, is
*(Scenario)* How many bits of entropy does a random 12-character password from the 94 printable ASCII characters have, approximately?
*(Scenario)* Which has the most entropy (all random)?
o: 6 words from a list of 7776 words (Diceware)
items.w: Six Diceware words give about 77.5 bits, against 37.6, 35.7 and 33.2 bits for the others.

items.q: *(Scenario)* An attacker tests 10 billion guesses per second against an unsalted fast hash of an 8-character random password from 62 letters and digits. The worst case time to try them all is about
items.w: 62^8 ≈ 2.18 × 10^14 guesses / 10^10 per second ≈ 21,800 seconds, which is about 6 hours.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which password policy is recommended by NIST SP 800-63B?
o: check against breached-password lists and allow long passphrases, without forced periodic changes
require one symbol and one capital letter
items.w: Frequent forced changes lead to predictable variations. Length and blocking known-bad passwords work better.

items.q: *(Recall)* "Peppering" passwords means
o: mixing in a secret kept outside the database, such as in an HSM or secret store
adding a random value to each hash row
items.w: If only the database leaks, the pepper is missing and offline cracking is much harder.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A developer writes `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(password.getBytes())` to store a password. What is wrong?
o: it is fast and unsalted, so the hash can be attacked at huge speed, use BCryptPasswordEncoder or Argon2
items.w: A password hash must be slow and salted. SHA-256 alone is designed to be fast.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A repository contains `private static final String KEY = "my-secret-key-123";` used for AES encryption. The main issue is
o: the key is hard-coded in source code and visible to anyone with the repository
items.w: Keys belong in a secret manager or KMS and must be rotated. Anything committed to version control must be treated as exposed.

items.question: Why is Base64 not a way to protect a password?
items.answer: Base64 is an encoding with no key. Anyone can decode it instantly.

items.question: How many hex characters does a SHA-256 digest have, and why is MD5 unsuitable for signatures?
items.answer: 64 hex characters (256 bits). MD5 is broken for collisions, so an attacker can create two different documents with the same hash.

items.question: What is the problem with AES in ECB mode?
items.answer: Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, so patterns in the data remain visible. Use GCM or another authenticated mode.

items.question: Alice wants to send Bob a secret that only Bob can read, and Bob wants to know it came from Alice. Which keys are involved?
items.answer: Alice encrypts with Bob's public key (so only Bob can decrypt) and signs with her own private key (so Bob can verify with Alice's public key).

items.question: Compute the toy RSA ciphertext of m = 65 with n = 3233 and e = 17, and say what the private exponent is.
items.answer: c = 65^17 mod 3233 = 2790. The private exponent is d = 2753.

items.question: Why do we salt passwords?
items.answer: The salt makes identical passwords produce different hashes, so precomputed rainbow tables fail and cracking one hash gives no clue about another.
